newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien says confident of majority.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien says confident of majority.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, despite an erosion of support in opinion polls, said on Wednesday he was confident his Liberals would win another majority government.

"We are very confident we will form a government," he told reporters at a rally in Edmonton, the only Alberta city that elected Liberals to Parliament in the 1993 election. "We will have a majority government. That is my goal. That is what I'm asking the Canadian people, and the indications are there."

Polls this week have showed a steady drop in the Liberals' still substantial national lead and regional differences have raised the question whether the Liberals might lose their majority in the House of Commons.

Asked about that prospect, Chretien said: "It would make life a bit more difficult but I don't think we'll have a minority government because the people of Canada think that they need a good government to finish the job."

A daily tracking poll on Wednesday conducted for Reuters by Zogby International showed Liberal support falling to 39.7 percent -- below the key 40 percent level for the first time. "If the tracking poll trends continue, Chretien may not win a majority," pollster John Zogby said.
When Parliament was dissolved the Liberals held 174 of 295 seats and were hoping to expand their showing in Alberta and British Columbia, where they held only 10 out of 58 seats.

The right-wing Reform Party, pressing for more conservative policies while feeding on discontent with the dominance of Quebec politicians, has maintained its support in its Western Canada electoral base.

Quebec-based Finance Minister Paul Martin, who has won international respect for slashing Canada's deficits, gave a fiery introduction to Chretien at a breakfast rally in Edmonton, urging voters to elect Liberals to finish the job.
"Canada is now on the brink of its greatest success," Martin said. "The deficit is on its way out. The stronger economy is on its way in."

Chretien's main support is in the east, especially Ontario, Canada's most populous province, where he was headed for a sweep of most of its 103 seats in the new Parliament. The Liberals won 98 of 99 seats contested in Ontario in 1993.

Chretien also voiced optimism for Liberal prospects in the second biggest province, Quebec, where the secessionist Bloc Quebecois has lost support. "The situation is very good for us. We'll increase the number of seats I'm sure. We'll do much better than last time," he said of Quebec.
In 1993, the Bloc Quebecois won 54 of Quebec's 75 seats, versus 19 for the Liberals and one for the Conservatives.
After a three-day Western Canada swing, Chretien was flying on Wednesday to a district in northern Ontario.
